meta.title: Hybrid Retrieval and RRF
meta.thesis: Hybrid Retrieval and RRF is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A search feature must combine exact keyword matches with semantic matches for product docs. By the end, they should be able to build or review hybrid retrieval plan using BM25, vectors, and reciprocal rank fusion, measure top-k recall across exact and paraphrased questions, and catch the failure where vector search misses exact version numbers while keyword search misses paraphrases.

mentalMap.title: Hybrid Retrieval and RRF: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Combine lexical exactness and dense semantic recall, then fuse rankings with a method that does not pretend scores are comparable.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Hybrid retrieval uses multiple imperfect search signals so exact identifiers and paraphrased intent can both reach the generator.

modules.title: Dense and sparse fail differently
modules.sub: Hybrid search starts by respecting each retriever’s strengths.
modules.summary: Vector search and keyword search are complementary, not rivals.
objectives: Explain why dense retrieval helps paraphrase.
Explain why BM25 helps exact terms and identifiers.
Recognize mixed queries that need both.

blocks.title: Two signals catch two kinds of relevance

spans.text: Problem anchor: a learner asks “Why does HNSW index creation fail for vector(1536)?” Dense search finds general vector database notes, while lexical search finds the exact HNSW migration error. Neither path alone is dependable.

Sparse retrieval rewards literal overlap: product names, stack traces, model IDs, legal clauses, and version numbers. Dense retrieval rewards meaning: “cite sources” can match “provenance,” and “wrong answer from docs” can match “retrieval miss.”
Label each term in a query as exact, semantic, or filter-worthy before choosing a retriever.

blocks.analogy: Dense search hears the melody; sparse search reads the sheet music.

blocks.title: Case study: API error code plus plain-English intent

spans.text: A docs assistant receives “How do I fix ERR_EMBED_DIM after switching bge-small to text-embedding-3-small?” The exact code and model names matter, but the user also wants migration guidance.
Sparse search catches ERR_EMBED_DIM and model names. Dense search catches the migration explanation even if it says “dimension mismatch.” RRF lets both pieces compete fairly.

items.text: Run dense retrieval for semantic migration context.
Run sparse retrieval for exact error and model identifiers.
Fuse by rank rather than raw score.
Inspect whether the fused top-k contains both diagnosis and fix.

blocks.title: Signal diagnosis
blocks.prompt: A vector retriever misses an exact error code. What is the most direct retrieval fix?

options.text: Increase model temperature.
Add or tune a sparse lexical path and fuse it with dense results.
Remove exact identifiers from documents.

blocks.explanation: The error code is a lexical signal; generation settings cannot retrieve it.

modules.title: RRF fuses ranks, not scores
modules.sub: Reciprocal rank fusion avoids score-scale mismatches.
modules.summary: RRF rewards documents that appear near the top of one or more retrieval lists.
objectives: Explain why raw dense and sparse scores should not be added blindly.
Tune top-k and deduplication for fused lists.

blocks.title: The rank is the common currency

spans.text: BM25 scores and vector similarities are produced by different systems. A score of 12.4 from one index and 0.78 from another do not mean comparable confidence. RRF sidesteps that by using rank position.
A common form adds 1/(k + rank) for each list. The constant k smooths the contribution so the first few ranks matter without making lower ranks worthless.
If the same chunk appears through both paths, dedupe it before generation but keep the evidence that both retrievers agreed.

blocks.analogy: RRF is a voting rule: each retriever submits an ordered ballot.

blocks.title: Worked fusion: dense finds meaning, sparse finds the symbol

spans.text: Dense top three: migration guide, vector dimensions note, pgvector overview. Sparse top three: ERR_EMBED_DIM troubleshooting, vector dimensions note, changelog.

RRF lifts “vector dimensions note” because both retrievers ranked it, while still keeping the exact troubleshooting page and the broader migration guide. The final set is better than either list alone.

items.text: Assign each hit a stable chunk ID.
For every retrieval list, add reciprocal-rank points by position.
Merge duplicate chunk IDs by summed score.
Sort fused scores and pass a bounded candidate set to reranking or prompt packing.

blocks.title: Fusion math
blocks.prompt: Why is RRF often safer than adding dense and BM25 scores directly?

options.text: It asks the LLM to rewrite every document.
It uses rank positions, so it avoids incompatible score scales.
It removes the need for deduplication.

blocks.explanation: Fusion still needs dedupe and evaluation; it just avoids score-unit confusion.

modules.title: Filters and analyzers decide what enters the race
modules.sub: Hybrid retrieval still needs metadata and lexical tuning.
modules.summary: Good fusion starts with eligible candidates.
objectives: Tune analyzers for symbols, casing, and code.
Explain how filters interact with dense recall.

blocks.title: Hybrid is not a substitute for eligibility

spans.text: A fused ranker should not decide whether a learner is allowed to see a source. Tenant, language, product, date, and document status filters belong before scoring.

Sparse analyzers also matter. Lowercasing may help ordinary prose but damage case-sensitive code symbols. Tokenizing on punctuation may break API names. These choices decide whether exact search really catches exactness.
If a query includes a version number, make the expected version a filter or a strongly preserved lexical token.

blocks.analogy: Before judging the race, make sure only eligible runners are on the track.

options.name: Metadata filter first

cells.text: Apply tenant, product, status, and version constraints before search.
Documents have permissions or versioned facts.
Overly strict filters can hide valid evidence.

options.whenToUse: Use as the default for production KBs.

options.name: Analyzer tuning

cells.text: Preserve symbols, casing, hyphens, and model IDs.
Queries include code, APIs, SKUs, or error strings.
Bad analyzers make sparse search look worse than it is.

options.whenToUse: Use for technical docs and logs.

options.name: Dense top-k expansion

cells.text: Retrieve more semantic candidates before fusion.
More candidates increase latency and reranking cost.

options.whenToUse: Use after checking filters and chunk quality.

blocks.title: Eligibility check
blocks.prompt: Hybrid retrieval returns a highly relevant chunk from a private customer document. What failed first?

options.text: RRF always leaks private chunks.
Eligibility filtering or permission metadata, not the fusion formula.
The model should ignore private text automatically.

blocks.explanation: Retrieval must prevent unauthorized evidence from reaching the prompt.

modules.title: Implement RRF in a small test harness
modules.sub: A few lines can expose duplicate handling and rank effects.
modules.summary: Hybrid retrieval becomes understandable when you can print the fused list.
objectives: Implement RRF over lists of chunk IDs.
Predict which chunks rise after agreement.

blocks.title: RRF is simple enough to unit test

spans.text: A production stack may involve vector stores, full-text indexes, and rerankers, but the fusion step should be small and deterministic. Keep it separate so you can test duplicate IDs and rank effects.
Spaced recall: from chunking, remember that chunk IDs must be stable. Fusion depends on stable IDs to dedupe dense and sparse hits.
If a chunk appears twice because overlap created near-duplicates with different IDs, fix chunk identity or dedupe by source span.

blocks.title: Runnable RRF over dense and sparse hit IDs
blocks.explanation: The shared “vector-dimensions” chunk rises because both lists ranked it, while unique exact and semantic hits remain available.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it, predict whether “vector-dimensions” beats the first item from each individual list.
predictThenReveal.answer: With k=60, agreement helps but does not completely erase top-ranked unique hits; this is why you still evaluate the final packed top-k.

blocks.title: RRF implementation
blocks.prompt: What bug appears if dense and sparse use different chunk IDs for the same source span?

options.text: The LLM will automatically merge them before retrieval.
Fusion cannot recognize agreement, so duplicates crowd the candidate list.
The sparse retriever stops returning exact matches.

blocks.explanation: Stable identity is part of retrieval engineering.

modules.title: Evaluate hybrid retrieval by failure bucket
modules.sub: The metric should reveal which signal fixed which miss.
modules.summary: Hybrid retrieval is justified when it fixes known recall holes.
objectives: Create exactness and paraphrase eval buckets.
Measure packed top-k, not only candidate top-k.
Decide when reranking is worth the cost.

spans.text: Do not add sparse search because it sounds more production-grade. Add it because the eval set contains exact identifiers that dense search misses, or because sparse-only search misses paraphrased user intent.
A good report separates “dense found it,” “sparse found it,” “fusion found it,” and “none found it.” That tells you whether to tune analyzers, chunking, embeddings, or reranking.
If hybrid improves top-50 but not the top-6 that enter the prompt, the generator still cannot use the improvement.

blocks.title: Verify AI output after adding RRF

spans.text: A fused list should improve evidence, not just logs.

items.text: Exact identifier questions retrieve the expected source within the packed context budget.
Paraphrased questions still retrieve semantically relevant chunks after sparse results are added.
Duplicate chunks are removed without losing source agreement signals.
Permission, product, and version filters are applied before fusion.
Answer citations point to chunks that actually support the generated sentences.

blocks.title: Hybrid release bar
blocks.prompt: Hybrid retrieval improves top-30 recall but not top-6 answer evidence. What should you inspect next?

options.text: The UI color of citation links.
Reranking, prompt packing, and whether fused candidates are being trimmed before generation.
Whether the model can memorize the missing document.

blocks.explanation: The model only sees what the final packing stage sends.

rag.label: RAG
rag.laymanDefinition: Retrieving relevant evidence before generation so answers can be grounded in sources.
rag.technicalNote: RAG quality depends on corpus freshness, chunking, embeddings, filters, ranking, citation handling, and faithfulness evaluation.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.laymanDefinition: A numeric vector representation of text used for semantic comparison.
embedding.technicalNote: Embedding choices fix dimension, distance metric, query/passage formatting, model version, and migration requirements for retrieval.

vector_search.label: Vector search
vector_search.laymanDefinition: Finding nearby vectors to retrieve semantically related chunks.
vector_search.technicalNote: Vector search needs metadata filters, recall tests, index tuning, and fallback for exact terms, IDs, and rare phrases.

chunk.label: Chunk
chunk.laymanDefinition: A source text segment stored and retrieved as a unit.
chunk.technicalNote: Chunk design balances semantic completeness, citation accuracy, token budget, overlap, metadata, and update/delete behavior.

reranker.label: Reranker
reranker.laymanDefinition: A second-stage model or method that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance.
reranker.technicalNote: Rerankers improve top-result precision when candidate recall is adequate, but add latency, cost, and evaluation complexity.

rrf.label: RRF
rrf.laymanDefinition: A rank-fusion method that merges multiple result lists by reciprocal rank.
rrf.technicalNote: RRF is useful for hybrid retrieval because it combines lexical and vector rankings without requiring comparable raw scores.

decisionDoc.title: Decision prompts for Hybrid Retrieval and RRF

questions.q: When should a RAG system add sparse search and RRF instead of tuning embeddings only?
questions.why: Dense search can miss exact names, versions, and error codes even while finding semantically related passages.
opts: Dense plus BM25 fused with RRF
questions.rot: Add hybrid retrieval when real queries contain identifiers or when the right answer appears in one retriever but not consistently near the top.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: From memory: which query is the strongest signal that hybrid retrieval is needed rather than dense-only or BM25-only?

options.text: “How do I reset my password?”
“timeout in createInvoiceV2 when user_id is null”
“What are the benefits of caching?”
“Explain retrieval augmented generation in simple terms.”

questions.explanation: The query mixes paraphrasable intent with exact identifiers like createInvoiceV2 and user_id, so dense and sparse retrieval can each catch different evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is Reciprocal Rank Fusion a safer default than directly adding BM25 scores to dense similarity scores?

options.text: RRF uses each retriever’s rank positions, avoiding assumptions that their raw scores mean the same thing.
RRF converts every document into a vector before ranking.
RRF always removes the need for metadata filters.
RRF guarantees the dense retriever and BM25 return identical top-k lists.

questions.explanation: Dense and sparse scores are on different scales, while RRF only needs each system’s ordering of results.

questions.prompt: You have tenant_id and product_version metadata, plus a query containing code symbols like `foo_bar()`; what setup best controls what can rank in the hybrid pipeline?

options.text: Run dense retrieval over all chunks, then filter tenant_id only after reranking.
Apply metadata filters before ranking and tune the sparse analyzer so symbols/casing/code tokens are preserved as needed.
Disable BM25 because analyzers cannot affect exact matching.
Remove filters to maximize recall, then trust RRF to ignore wrong-tenant chunks.

questions.explanation: Pre-ranking filters keep ineligible chunks out of the race, and analyzer choices determine whether exact symbolic terms can be matched.

questions.prompt: In a small RRF test harness, if chunk A ranks 2nd in dense and 3rd in sparse while chunk B ranks 1st in dense but is absent from sparse, which chunk would you generally expect to rise more after fusion, and why?
questions.acceptableAnswer: Chunk A, because RRF rewards agreement across lists; appearing reasonably high in both dense and sparse can beat a chunk that appears in only one list, depending on the RRF constant and other ranks.
questions.explanation: RRF gives points from each ranked list, so cross-retriever agreement is often boosted above one-list-only strength.

questions.prompt: When evaluating whether reranking is worth adding after hybrid retrieval, which measurement plan best matches the lesson?

options.text: Use only one aggregate accuracy number over all queries and tune until it improves.
Track exactness and paraphrase failure buckets, measure the packed top-k shown to the model, and add reranking only if it fixes remaining high-value failures enough to justify cost.
Measure candidate top-k before deduplication because that is the largest list.
Skip evaluation buckets if RRF is implemented correctly.

questions.explanation: Hybrid retrieval should be judged by the failure modes it is meant to fix and by the final packed context, not just raw candidates.
